text.p: British manufacturing output rose for the fifth month in a row in October to its highest level in 18 months, a business group said Friday.
The Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply said October also saw the first significant increase in manufacturing employment since March 1995.
Its purchasing managers' index (PMI) rose to a seasonally adjusted 54.5 percent in October from 53.5 percent in September.

"The latest rise in output was driven by an increase in the rate of growth of new orders. This was the fifth successive monthly improvement in order books and, as in recent months, orders for consumer goods showed the greatest increase," the CIPS said.
The survey, based on questionnaires sent to 310 industrial companies, is seen as an accurate barometer of developments in manufacturing that are usually reflected in later official statistics.
Prices fell overall in October, but the survey showed "tentative signs of a tightening of price and supply conditions."
The October survey was conducted before the unexpected quarter-point increase in official interest rates to 6.0 percent on Wednesday, meant to ward off inflation as economic growth gathers steam.
Economists said the rate rise, which sent the pound soaring to a 2-1/2 year high on foreign exchange markets, could make life harder for manufacturers in the coming months.
"The upturn is still quite modest and the strength of the pound will be doing manufacturers no favours at all -- neither will the base rate hike," said Jonathan Loynes, economist at HSBC Markets.
A stronger pound makes British exports more expensive overseas and higher rates raise companies' costs of doing business and tend to slow the economy.
Some economists have warned the government that the financial stability it achieved in the early and mid-1990s would be in jeopardy if it did not cut borrowing and raise interest rates further.
